_about: Good/bad passage pairs from William Fitzpatrick (Writer Science) video cayUBPHB1HQ and the writerscience.com Writing Tools library. Verdicts are the source author's own. Used as ground truth for the flow linter. Tier author = verdict from the Writer Science source. Tier panel = passages written by workflow judges, verdicts are theirs, reported separately.

fixtures.text: Happiness is not something that happens. It is not the result of good fortune or random chance. It is not something that money can buy or power command. It does not depend on outside events, but rather on how we interpret them. Happiness, in fact, is a condition that must be prepared for, cultivated, and defended privately by each person.

fixtures.source: Fitzpatrick's unpublished rewrite, nothing removed (video 1:33, slide 1:40)
fixtures.text: Things that happen are not what produces happiness. Good fortune and random chance don't result in it, either. Money can't buy it, and power can't command it. Outside events do not determine it; our interpretation of those events does. Preparation, cultivation, and private defence by each person are what this condition requires.

fixtures.source: Jonathan Haidt, The Righteous Mind (video 19:26, slide 19:40)
topics_in_order: In their theory of morality, Shweder et al.
fixtures.text: In their theory of morality, Shweder et al. found three major clusters of moral themes, which they called the ethics of autonomy, community, and divinity. The ethic of autonomy is based on the idea that people are, first and foremost, autonomous individuals with wants, needs, and preferences. The ethic of community is based on the idea that people are, first and foremost, members of larger entities such as families, teams, armies, companies, tribes, and nations. The ethic of divinity is based on the idea that people are, first and foremost, temporary vessels within which a divine soul has been implanted.

fixtures.text: Clear visual hierarchy at the top of web pages helps visitors identify what a site is primarily for. A sense of usability emerges when a series of menu items reflects a limited set of core functions. But the purpose of each page is obscured by apparently arbitrary changes of navigation. Confusing websites result when that happens.

fixtures.source: writerscience.com Coherence tool, member section, revised version
topics_in_order: But when navigation seems to change arbitrarily, visitors
fixtures.text: Visitors identify what a site is primarily for when they see clear visual hierarchy at the top of web pages, especially in the main headings. They feel a site is usable when they encounter a series of menu items that reflects a limited set of core functions. But when navigation seems to change arbitrarily, visitors lose track of each page's purpose. When that happens, they feel they are using a website that is confusing and even poorly designed.

the first Russian atom bomb test

fixtures.text: Many issues other than science, domestic politics in particular, faced Truman when he was considering the Oppenheimer committee's recommendation to stop the hydrogen bomb project. A Sino-Soviet bloc had been proclaimed by Russia and China, so the Cold War was becoming an issue. Support for Truman's foreign policy was shrinking among Republican leaders in Congress. And the first Russian atom bomb test made the public demand a strong response from him. Truman's conclusion that he could not afford letting the public think that Russia had been allowed to be the first in developing the most powerful weapon yet was an inevitable one. The risk in the Oppenheimer recommendation was worth taking, according to some historians, but the political issues that Truman had to face were too powerful to ignore.
fixtures.note: The first sentence has a 9-word runway. The cap is 10 because Pinker's good passage carries a 10-word subject with an appositive.

fixtures.source: Follow-up video n1CrHXxcfbA, rewrite built on screen 4:00 to 11:30; transcribed from speech, wording reconstructed
topics_in_order: When Truman was considering the Oppenheimer committee's recommendation to stop the hydrogen bomb project, he
Third, since the Russians had been first to test the atom bomb, the public
fixtures.text: When Truman was considering the Oppenheimer committee's recommendation to stop the hydrogen bomb project, he was faced with many issues other than science, domestic politics in particular. First, Russia and China had proclaimed a Sino-Soviet bloc, making the Cold War an issue. Second, Truman's foreign policy was losing support from Republican leaders in Congress. Third, since the Russians had been first to test the atom bomb, the public demanded his strong response. Truman inevitably concluded that he could not afford letting the public think that Russia had been allowed to be first in developing the most powerful weapon yet. According to some historians, Truman should have risked following the Oppenheimer recommendation. But Truman could not ignore these powerful political issues.
